hops.title: The C fibres that sense gentle touch
hops.text: Glide a fingertip down the hairy back of your forearm twice: once from elbow to wrist in half a second, then again taking three seconds to cross ten centimeters. You can also compare the two speeds with someone else stroking your forearm. Hairy skin carries unmyelinated C-tactile fibres, axons of low-threshold sensory neurons tuned to gentle touch rather than pain. Single-fibre human recordings show they fire hardest during soft strokes between one and ten centimeters per second, the speeds people rate as most pleasant. When volunteers stroked their partner or their baby, all used speeds suited to those fibres; the artificial-arm group stroked faster on average.

sources.citation: Loken, Wessberg, Morrison, McGlone & Olausson, Nature Neuroscience 12(5):547-548 (2009), PMID 19363489.
Croy, Luong, Triscoli, Hofmann, Olausson & Sailer, Behavioural Brain Research 297:37-40 (2016), PMID 26433145.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student at a wooden desk gently stroking the back of their forearm with one fingertip.
image.caption: C-tactile fibres in hairy skin fire hardest to gentle strokes, around one to ten centimeters per second.

hops.afterHeading: From a candidate cluster to a functional test
hops.title: Cre lines named for neurons that edit sperm and eggs
hops.text: It is tempting to read a Cre line named for the nervous system as editing only neurons. In 2020, a team pooled data on 64 widely used nervous-system Cre lines; 41 showed some germline recombination. When Cre is active in cells that become sperm or eggs, a pup can inherit an already recombined allele, and which parent carries Cre can change the odds. In one forebrain interneuron line, 29 of 34 Cre-negative pups from Cre-carrying mothers inherited a recombined Clstn3 allele; none from Cre-carrying fathers did. In a separate maternal cross, 6 of 18 Cre-negative pups that inherited a reporter allele had it recombined: recombination rates can differ by locus.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A puzzled white lab mouse inspecting its glowing paw with a magnifying glass beneath two silhouetted adult mice.
image.caption: Most tested nervous-system Cre lines showed germline recombination, so specificity has to be measured.

hops.afterHeading: When subtype identity changes: development and injury
hops.title: The naked mole-rat's hypofunctional TrkA
hops.text: Underground in equatorial East Africa, the naked mole-rat runs its own version of the NGF experiment. Unlike mice and rats, naked mole-rats develop no heat hypersensitivity after NGF, even though their TRPV1 heat-sensing channels work normally. In 2016, researchers linked that to weaker signalling from the TrkA kinase domain, pointing to one to three amino-acid substitutions as possible contributors. The receptor still looks sufficient for developing sensory neurons: the team counted substantially more unmyelinated C fibres in two leg nerves from three-day-old pups than in the corresponding adult nerves. Weak signalling is their candidate explanation for how few cutaneous C fibres adults keep.

sources.citation: Omerbasic et al., Cell Reports 17(3):748-758 (2016), PMID 27732851, PMCID PMC5081396.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A pink wrinkled naked mole-rat peeking out of an underground dirt burrow.
image.caption: Weak TrkA signalling helps explain why NGF fails to make naked mole-rats more sensitive to painful heat.
